newsitem.title: USA: Malaysia seeks broader ties with U.S. business.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia seeks broader ties with U.S. business.

text.p: Malaysia is eager to find more U.S. companies, including small and mid-sized firms, to export everything from helicopters to frozen french fries, Malaysian officials said Wednesday.

"I cannot overemphasize the importance of having a physical presence in Malaysia" to tap into the Asia-Pacific region's booming economies, Malaysia's ambassador to the United States, Dali M. Hashim, told Reuters in an interview.
One of Mahathir's pet projects is the vaunted Multimedia Super Corridor, a 15-km by 50-km (nine miles by 30 miles) information technology hub, Hashim said.

Malaysia would like U.S. companies to have a big presence in the zone, which stretches south from Kuala Lumpur to an area where a new "paperless" federal capital and a "cyberspace" international airport are also under construction.

Malaysia, with a population of 19 million, is the 11th biggest trading partner of the United States, and ranks 17th among the U.S. export markets -- bigger than India and Russia combined, Hashim said.
The ambassador was in Connecticut to launch a U.S. tour by Malaysian officials.
Among the country's ties with Connecticut is Kuala Lumpur's Petronas Towers, which last year took over the distinction of being the world's tallest building, at 452 metres (1,482 feet).

The futuristic towers were designed by Cesar Pelli Associates of New Haven, Connecticut, and its $80 million elevators were built by Farmington, Connecticut-based Otis Elevator Co., a unit of United Technologies Corp.

The state's ties with Malaysia also extend to the world's biggest casino, Foxwoods, which opened in Ledyard, Connecticut, in 1992. It was Malaysian property tycoon Lim Goh Tong who provided the loan to Connecticut's Mashantucket Pequot Indian tribe to build the casino and resort, Hashim said.
Hartford-based Aetna Inc is the third-biggest life insurer in Malaysia, said C.H. Saw, Malaysia's consul general to the U.S.
Malaysia's financial services sector, including insurance, will be fully opened up in 1999, he said.
Hashim said Malaysia no longer sold itself as a bastion of cheap labor. In fact, the country has virtually no unemployment and is dependent upon foreign labor.
Malaysia is looking for capital investment, import of advanced goods and partnerships to market products in the dynamic southeast Asian economies, Hashim said.
He said there are vast opportunities in telecommunications, road development, rail transport, energy, agriculture, medical equipment, franchises, and environmental products.
Despite Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's frequent criticisms of the West, Malaysia views increased U.S. investment as critical to its drive to become fully developed within 25 years, Hashim said.
"Unfortunately, his criticisms of the West have been highlighted," the ambassador said.

Mahathir, 71, has feuded with Australia and Britain in recent years and has often criticized "Western values" as incompatible with predominantly Moslem Malaysia. He has served as prime minister since 1981.
